newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco's opposition mobilises activists for polls.
newsitem.headline: Morocco's opposition mobilises activists for polls.

text.p: Morocco's opposition, including the old guard Istiqlal party, moved into the last two days of campaigning with activists mobilised to attract voters for the local elections on June 13.

"Opposition leaders are expected to hold more than 50 meetings throughout the country in the next 48 hours to mobilise public opinion on the need for political change," an Istiqlal spokesman told Reuters.

The four main opposition parties, grouped in a bloc known as the Koutla Addimocratia (democratic bloc), are fielding a total of 33,987 candidates. The parties are the Istiqlal, formed in the early 1940s, USFP, PPS and the Organisation of Democratic and Popular Action (OADP).

"Friday's elections have a great importance for our present and future...We (opposition) are obliged to concentrate our efforts to avoid past experiences," USFP leader Abderrahman Youssoufi told Moroccan RTM television, referring to what the opposition term the "previous unfair elections".
Youssoufi was among political leaders using radio and TV broadcasts to call on the 13 million Moroccan voters to support them.
Pro-government parties have dominated local polls since the begining of 1960s because of what another USFP leader said was "the administration's support and manipulation of results".
"For the first time in Morocco's modern history, the opposition is showing real confidence in mobilising the maximum number of voters in the coming elections," a Western diplomat said.
He pointed out they had also chosen more women as their candidates compared with the past elections.
Interior ministry figures show a total 6,600 women competing with more than 94,000 men for about 25,000 council seats.
During the past 13 days of campaigning, politicians have sought to galvanise voters but to little effect, according to local commentators.
One independent Moroccan analyst said on Wednesday: "There are no signs that people are excited to join mass rallies."

The local elections are the first of a series which will culminate in parliamentary elections in September, with a new bicameral parliament being inaugurated by King Hassan on the second Friday of October.

Under the new constitution, the Lower House of parliament will be directly elected through universal suffrage. Local councils will elect three-fifths of the members of a new Upper House being set up under constitutional reforms approved last September.
The Upper House will have power to vote a no-confidence motion in the government and could topple it.
